Where a name ranks — forward and trailing P/E

Forward (NTM) and trailing (TTM) consensus P/E for 3003 US companies — the S&P 500 and the Russell 1000 / 2000 / 3000 — cut into quintiles over whichever universe you choose. Prices as of 2026-09-25 · built 2026-09-25 · back to the weekly chart pack
The file is still called sp500_valuation.html so the existing link and bookmark keep working; the scope grew, the URL deliberately did not.

653 of 3003 names are not ranked (558 negative forward EPS · 91 no forward consensus · 4 no price). They are listed at the bottom and are excluded from the quintile cut rather than parked at the expensive end.
Index membership. Russell 1000 1022 names, as of 2026-09-23 (2d old) via IWB  ·  Russell 2000 1976 names, as of 2026-09-23 (2d old) via IWM  ·  Russell 3000 2998 names, as of 2026-09-23 (2d old) via IWB+IWM. Russell membership comes from iShares' published holdings — IWB for the Russell 1000 and IWM for the Russell 2000, both full-replication funds; FTSE Russell sells the lists, so a fund that tracks the index is the free route. The Russell 3000 is the two combined (iShares' own Russell 3000 fund is sampled, so it is not used). S&P 500 membership is Coverage Manager's cached Wikipedia list as of 2026-09-18. Membership is not priced daily — these dates lag the prices above, and Russell reconstitutes once a year in June.
Two sector authorities, and the rows say which. 503 names carry their real GICS sector (the S&P 500 list); 2478 carry FMP's sector mapped onto the GICS label, and 22 have none. Measured on the 501 names that carry both, the two agree 94.4% of the time and disagree on 5.6% — mostly payment processors GICS moved to Financials in 2023, and packaging. A sector board is therefore a near-GICS board, not a GICS board.
What this answers. Not "is this dear versus its own history" — the pack already does that — but "is this dear versus other stocks, today". Those are different claims with very different evidence behind them: a 2016 CRSP/Compustat study puts cross-sectional value at 5.50%/yr gross long-short (1990–2014) against 1.25%/yr for the own-history version. Cheap is coloured green here because that is the direction the cross-sectional evidence points; the same green on the pack's own-history view is a far weaker claim.

The quintile board

Q1 is the cheapest fifth on the chosen multiple, Q5 the dearest. The universe cuts the quintiles; the filter beneath it only hides rows — and the line at the top of the page always says which view you are in. A • marks a name in your own book. Click any ticker to pin it.

All names

Click a column header to sort. Mkt Q (headed Univ Q under a sector universe) is the quintile across the selected universe; Sec Q is the quintile within the name's own GICS sector — both are shown because a bank at 12x and a software name at 12x are not the same fact, and neither column alone says so. Pctile is the percentile of NTM P/E ascending within the ranked universe: 5 means only 5% of that universe is cheaper.

Index-level multiples

Two different questions, both answered. Aggregate is total market value ÷ total earnings — the cap-weighted multiple, i.e. what the index itself costs, where the mega-caps vote their weight. Median is the middle constituent, which is what the quintile boundaries above are cut from. On this run they differ by more than a point, and neither is a substitute for the other.

Where the aggregate reads n/m — Russell 2000, trailing: index earnings are negative (−$6B); 813 of 1961 members lose money, so there is no aggregate multiple. This is a property of the index, not a missing number: an index whose members collectively lose money has no aggregate multiple, and the median and the profitable-only aggregate are the readable figures for it.
How this is computed, and why it will not exactly equal a vendor's number. Market value is FMP's full market cap, not float-adjusted, while S&P weights the index on float — so this is a full-cap aggregate and runs a little different by construction. Multiple share classes of one issuer are collapsed first (FMP reports Alphabet's entire 82.4T-scale cap under both GOOGL and GOOG); leaving them in doubles that issuer's weight and moved the trailing aggregate by 3.1% on this run. Loss-makers are kept in the earnings sum, which is the honest index number — dropping them always reads cheaper. The pack's Global-equity-valuations section reports a separate S&P 500 trailing P/E from MSCI/Damodaran; this one is computed here from constituents. They are two independent derivations of the same idea and land within a few percent — do not net them against each other, and do not treat a gap between them as a market signal. This one is 0.6x trailing.

Cross-check against published index multiples

Same idea, four derivations. They will never be identical, and the reasons are listed in the last column — different index, different share-count basis, different date, and above all a different rule about loss-making companies. Read the column of reasons before reading the gap.

The gap has a name. Against IVV's 24.8x, this page reads -97.5% including loss-makers and -97.7% excluding them. The second number is the whole story: published index multiples drop companies that lose money, which always reads cheaper. Our two figures bracket the vendor's rather than disagreeing with it.
Do not net these against each other and do not read a moving gap between them as a market signal. They are independent derivations, and a change in one can be a change of vintage or convention rather than of price. The pack applies the same rule to its own international rows, where crossing a trailing multiple with a forward average invented ~17 points of richness out of the definition alone.
Method. NTM P/E = price ÷ NTM consensus EPS, where NTM EPS blends the consensus FY1 and FY2 annual EPS by the time remaining in FY1: w = days to FY1 end / 365, NTM EPS = w·FY1 + (1−w)·FY2. The blend is not a refinement — fiscal years end in different months, so a raw FY1 multiple compares a company eleven months into its year against one that is one month in, and the ranking would inherit that error.
Sources. Consensus EPS: FMP /stable/analyst-estimates (annual). Price and market cap: FMP /stable/quote. Constituents, company names and GICS sectors: Coverage Manager's cached Wikipedia list. All refreshed by the same Friday job that builds the weekly pack.
What this is not. It is a snapshot of embedded expectations, not a return forecast and not a buy list. A low multiple is frequently correct pricing of a deteriorating business, and consensus EPS is a lagging object — a name that has just guided down can print a flatteringly low multiple until estimates catch up. Cross-sector comparison on P/E alone is unsound, which is why the sector quintile sits beside the market one.
